Below is a short “tourist‑guide” of the most interesting sights you’ll pass (or can easily step off the path) on the 1‑km walk from **Tiananmen Square** to **The Palace Museum (Forbidden City)**.  
All distances are measured from the **center of Tiananmen Square** (the big open plaza where the flag‑raising ceremony takes place) and the walking times are approximate for an average‑pace visitor (≈ 5 km/h).  

| # | Spot | Approx. distance from Tiananmen Square | How to get there from the route | What to see / why it’s worth a stop | Typical visit time |
|---|------|----------------------------------------|--------------------------------|------------------------------------|--------------------|
| 1 | **Tiananmen Square (天安门广场)** | 0 m (starting point) | – | The world’s largest city square, the site of the 1949 founding ceremony of the People’s Republic of China. Look up the **Monument to the People’s Heroes** and the massive **National Flag**. | 10‑15 min (photo‑ops) |
| 2 | **Monument to the People’s Heroes (人民英雄纪念碑)** | 30 m north of the square | Directly on the north side of the square, just before you reach the Gate of Heavenly Peace. | A 38‑m tall obelisk commemorating revolutionary martyrs; the base houses an exhibition of historic photographs. | 5‑10 min |
| 3 | **Gate of Heavenly Peace – Tiananmen (天安门)** | 70 m north of the square | Walk straight north; the gate is the iconic red‑arched entrance to the Forbidden City. | The grand ceremonial gate where state leaders address the nation. The massive portrait of Mao Zedong hangs above the central arch. | 5‑10 min |
| 4 | **National Museum of China (中国国家博物馆)** | 120 m north of the square, on the east side of the square | Turn right (east) from the gate and walk a few steps along the square’s edge. | China’s premier museum of art, archaeology and natural history. The main exhibition hall is open to the public; you can pop in for a quick look at the **Bronze Age artifacts** or the **Ming‑Qing porcelain**. | 15‑30 min (optional) |
| 5 | **Great Hall of the People (人民大会堂)** | 150 m north‑west of the square, on the west side | Walk along the north side of the square, then veer left (west) toward the massive white‑marble building. | The seat of the National People’s Congress. Its grand marble staircase and massive auditorium are impressive even from the outside. | 5 min (photo) |
| 6 | **Meridian Gate – Wu Men (午门)** | 300 m north of Tiananmen, the first gate of the Forbidden City | Continue straight north on the pedestrian path; you’ll reach the **Wu Men** after crossing the small “south‑gate” plaza. | The main entrance to the Forbidden City, with five arches and a massive bronze lion statue. | 5‑10 min |
| 7 | **Imperial Garden (御花园) – the inner courtyard of the Forbidden City** | Inside the Forbidden City, just beyond the Meridian Gate | After entering the Meridian Gate, follow the main north‑south axis; the garden lies at the very back of the palace complex. | A beautifully restored imperial garden with rockeries, ponds, and ancient trees. It offers a quiet contrast to the bustling streets. | 10‑15 min |
| 8 | **Jingshan Hill (景山公园) – “Prospect Hill”** | ~600 m west of the Meridian Gate (a short side‑street detour) | Exit the Forbidden City at the **North Gate (北门)**, walk west along **Jingshan Front Street**, then ascend the hill. | From the top you get a panoramic view of the Forbidden City’s rooftops and Tiananmen Square – one of the best photo spots in Beijing. | 15‑20 min (incl. climb) |
| 9 | **Beihai Park (北海公园)** | ~800 m southwest of the route (via Qianmen Street) | From the square, head south a few minutes to **Qianmen**, then walk west along **Beihai North Road**. | A classic imperial garden with a large lake, historic pavilions, and the famous **White Dagoba**. Great for a relaxing stroll after the palace. | 20‑30 min (optional) |
|10| **Zhongshan Park (中山公园)** | ~900 m north‑west of the route (just beyond the Forbidden City) | After exiting the north gate of the Forbidden City, walk a short distance west. | Formerly the imperial garden of the **Ming** and **Qing** dynasties, now a public park with ancient trees and a small museum. | 10‑15 min |
|11| **Wangfujing Shopping Street (王府井大街)** | ~1 km east of the route (a short side‑street walk) | From the east side of the square, walk east along **East Chang’an Avenue** and turn onto **Wangfujing**. | Beijing’s most famous pedestrian shopping street – perfect for a snack break (try the **stinky tofu** or **candied hawthorn**) or souvenir shopping. | 20‑40 min (optional) |

### How to Fit Them Into Your Walk

Because the core walk is only about **1 km (≈ 15 min)**, you can easily add a few of the highlights without turning the trip into a full‑day tour:

| Suggested “quick‑stop” itinerary (≈ 45 min) |
|--------------------------------------------|
| 1️⃣ Start at **Tiananmen Square** – photo of the flag and the square (5 min). |
| 2️⃣ Walk north to the **Monument to the People’s Heroes** (5 min). |
| 3️⃣ Pass the **Gate of Heavenly Peace** (quick photo, 3 min). |
| 4️⃣ Continue to the **Meridian Gate** of the Forbidden City (5 min). |
| 5️⃣ Enter the **Palace Museum** – you can buy a ticket and explore the **Hall of Supreme Harmony** and the **Imperial Garden** (≈ 20 min). |
| 6️⃣ Exit via the **North Gate**, climb a short stretch to **Jingshan Hill** for the classic skyline view (≈ 7 min). |
| 7️⃣ Return to the square or head to **Beihai Park** for a relaxing finish (optional). |

If you have a bit more time (1‑2 hours), you can also:

* Pop into the **National Museum of China** (free entry, quick 15‑minute glance).  
* Walk a few minutes west to **Beihai Park** for a lakeside stroll.  
* End the day with a snack on **Wangfujing**.

### Practical Tips

| Tip | Details |
|-----|---------|
| **Tickets** | The Palace Museum requires an entry ticket (usually ¥60 for adults). Buy online in advance to avoid the line. |
| **Opening hours** | Palace Museum: 8:30 am – 5:00 pm (last entry 4:10 pm). National Museum: 9:00 am – 5:00 pm (closed on Mondays). |
| **Footwear** | The walk is on paved sidewalks and stone steps inside the palace – comfortable walking shoes are recommended. |
| **Weather** | In summer, bring a hat and water; in winter, dress warmly – the north‑south axis can be windy. |
| **Navigation** | All the spots are within a 10‑minute walk of each other. A simple map app (Baidu Maps, Google Maps, or Apple Maps) with “walking” mode will keep you on the pedestrian‑only streets. |
| **Restrooms** | Public toilets are available at Tiananmen Square, the National Museum, and inside the Palace Museum (near the **Hall of Supreme Harmony**). |
| **Accessibility** | The main route is flat, but the **Jingshan Hill** climb involves many steps; a wheelchair‑friendly path is available on the western side of the hill. |

Enjoy your walk through the historic heart of Beijing! If you’d like a more detailed itinerary (e.g., exact opening‑hour schedules, ticket‑booking links, or a printable map), just let me know.

Below is a concise, easy‑to‑read description of every tag that appeared in the samples you asked about.  The definitions are written in plain language and include the typical behaviours or characteristics that security analysts associate with each tag.

| Tag | What it means (typical characteristics) |
|-----|------------------------------------------|
| **trojan** | A program that pretends to be legitimate software but secretly performs malicious actions (e.g., stealing credentials, opening a back‑door, downloading additional payloads).  Trojans do **not** self‑replicate; they rely on social engineering to get executed. |
| **ransomware** | Malware that encrypts a victim’s files (or locks the system) and then demands a payment—usually in cryptocurrency—to provide the decryption key.  Ransomware often drops a ransom note, contacts a C2 server, and may also exfiltrate data before encryption. |
| **Worm** | Self‑propagating malware that can spread automatically across networks, removable drives, or email without user interaction.  Worms typically exploit vulnerabilities or use weak credentials to move laterally. |
| **Infection** | A generic tag indicating that the sample is capable of infecting a host system.  It is often used together with more specific tags (e.g., “Worm”, “Trojan”) to highlight that the file can establish a foothold on a victim machine. |
| **High risk** | An advisory label used by analysts to flag a sample that is especially dangerous—e.g., it has a high detection rate, contains multiple malicious capabilities, or is known to be used in active campaigns.  It does **not** describe a technical behavior, but rather the overall threat level. |
| **Bank Trojan** | A specialized trojan that targets banking or financial applications.  It typically captures login credentials, injects malicious code into banking webpages, or performs man‑in‑the‑browser (MitB) attacks to steal money. |
| **Data theft** | Indicates that the sample is designed to exfiltrate sensitive information (credentials, documents, screenshots, etc.) from the infected host.  The tag is often paired with other categories (e.g., “trojan”, “bank trojan”). |
| **Malware** | The broad, umbrella term for any malicious software.  In many databases it is used as a generic tag when a more specific family or behavior has not yet been identified. |
| **adware** | Software that displays unwanted advertisements, often by hijacking the browser or injecting ads into legitimate applications.  While adware is usually less destructive than trojans or ransomware, it can be a delivery vector for more dangerous payloads and is considered unwanted. |
| **trojan** (duplicate entry) | See the first row – the same definition applies. |
| **malware** (duplicate entry) | See the “Malware” row – the same definition applies. |

### Quick reference summary

- **Trojan / Bank Trojan** – Disguised as legit software; steals data or credentials.  
- **Ransomware** – Encrypts files and demands payment.  
- **Worm** – Self‑spreads without user interaction.  
- **Infection** – General indicator that the file can compromise a system.  
- **High risk** – Analyst‑assigned severity flag; treat with extra caution.  
- **Data theft** – Focused on exfiltrating information.  
- **Adware** – Shows unwanted ads; can be a nuisance or a delivery method.  
- **Malware** – Generic catch‑all label for any malicious program.

These definitions should help you understand the threat landscape of the samples you retrieved. If you need deeper technical details (e.g., specific IOCs, C2 infrastructure, or mitigation steps) for any particular tag or sample, just let me know!

candidate_0_answer_function_list.observation:
The following are the meanings of common malware tags:

### Related to malware types
- **trojan**: A malicious program hidden within a normal program or file. It may appear harmless on the surface, but in fact, it will perform malicious operations without the user's knowledge. For example, stealing user data (such as passwords, credit card information), remotely controlling the user's device, and opening a backdoor for attackers to access.
 - **ransomware**: This type of malware encrypts important files or the entire storage system on the user's device and then demands a ransom from the user, usually in the form of virtual currencies such as Bitcoin, in exchange for the decryption key to restore the data.
 - **worm**: A malicious program that can self-replicate and spread automatically through networks (such as the Internet and local area networks). It can spread between different devices without user intervention, may consume a large amount of network resources, cause network congestion, and may also carry other malicious payloads.
 - **adware**: Software that displays a large number of advertisements on the user's device. It usually interferes with the normal use of the device by forcibly popping up advertisement windows, changing the browser homepage, and inserting advertisements into web pages. Some adware may also collect information such as the user's browsing habits for advertising purposes and may even be bundled with other malware.
 - **banker trojan**: A special type of trojan that specifically targets financial institutions and users' bank accounts. It can steal sensitive information such as the username and password entered by the user when logging in to online banking, and then transfer the funds in the user's account.

### Related to malicious behaviors
 - **infection**: Indicates that the malware has the ability to infect other files or system components. For example, it modifies normal executable files so that they also contain malicious code, thereby expanding the spread of the malware within the system.
 - **stealth**: Means that the main behavior of the malware is to secretly steal the user's sensitive information, such as personal identity information, financial information, login credentials, etc., and may send this information to the attacker.

### Related to risk levels
 - **high risk**: Indicates that the malware has a high probability of causing serious harm to the user's device and data, which may lead to major consequences such as data loss, system crashes, and privacy breaches. Immediate measures need to be taken to handle it.

### Related to association relationships
 - **variant**: Refers to a malicious program that is similar in code structure and function to a known malware but has some minor differences. Variants may be produced when attackers modify the original malware to evade detection, enhance malicious functions, or target specific targets.
 - **ancestor**: In the evolutionary relationship of malware, the ancestor malware is an earlier version within a malware family. Subsequent variants or related malware are developed based on it, and it often has some basic characteristics and functions of the malware family.

candidate_0_answer_function_list.observation:
The following is an introduction to the meanings of these security threat types: MALWARE, UNWANTED_SOFTWARE, and SOCIAL_ENGINEERING:
- **MALWARE (Malicious Software)**: 
    - **Definition**: Malicious software refers to the general term for software programs that are deliberately programmed or set with malicious purposes, such as aiming to damage the functions and data of computer systems or obtain users' private information. 
    - **Examples**: 
        - **Virus**: It can self-replicate and spread to other programs or files. For example, the once prevalent "Blaster" virus exploited vulnerabilities in the Windows system to spread, which could cause problems such as the system restarting repeatedly and running more slowly. 
        - **Worm**: It can run independently and spread automatically through the network. For instance, the "Nimda" worm virus could spread rapidly in the network, occupying a large amount of network bandwidth and affecting the normal use of the network. 
        - **Trojan Horse**: It disguises itself as a normal program or file to induce users to download and install it. Once it runs, it will perform malicious operations in the background, such as stealing users' account passwords and other information. For example, some Trojan programs disguised as popular games may steal users' account information after the users install them. 
- **UNWANTED_SOFTWARE (Unwanted Software)**: 
    - **Definition**: This type of software is usually not actively expected to be installed by users. They may be installed on devices without the users' knowledge or explicit consent and may bring various troubles and potential risks to users. 
    - **Examples**: 
        - **Adware**: It frequently pops up a large number of advertisement windows, interfering with the normal use of the device by users. These advertisements may occupy system resources, causing the device to run more slowly. Some advertisements may also pose security risks, and clicking on them may lead users to malicious websites. 
        - **Spyware**: It collects users' personal information, browsing habits and other data without the users' awareness and sends this data to third parties. For example, some spyware will record the search keywords entered by users in the browser, the websites visited, etc., infringing on users' privacy. 
        - **Bundled Software**: It is often installed bundled with the software that users actually need. For example, when users download a certain legitimate software, the installation package may be bundled with some other software. These bundled software may be useless in function or even pose security risks. 
- **SOCIAL_ENGINEERING (Social Engineering Attacks)**: 
    - **Definition**: It takes advantage of human psychological weaknesses, trust relationships, and behavioral habits. Through means such as deception and inducement, it obtains sensitive information (such as account passwords, bank card numbers, etc.) or gets users to perform certain operations that are not conducive to their own security. 
    - **Examples**: 
        - **Phishing Email**: The attacker disguises as a legitimate institution (such as a bank, a well-known company, etc.) and sends an email to the user. The email usually contains false links or attachments to induce the user to click. For example, a phishing email disguised as a bank will claim that there is a problem with the user's account and ask the user to click on the link to log in to the "bank website" to modify the information. And this link points to a forged website used to steal the user's account password. 
        - **Telephone Fraud**: The fraudster calls the user, fabricating various reasons (such as winning a prize, being suspected of illegal crimes, etc.) to induce the user to transfer money or disclose personal sensitive information. For example, the scammer calls and claims that the user has won a huge prize, but needs to pay a certain handling fee first to receive the bonus, inducing the user to transfer money. 
        - **Impersonating Customer Service**: The attacker impersonates the customer service staff of a well-known e-commerce platform or other services to contact the user. Under the pretext of solving problems, they obtain the user's account information or defraud money. For example, impersonating a customer service of an e-commerce platform and claiming that there is a problem with the user's order and needs to be refunded, guiding the user to click on a link to operate, but actually defrauding the user's funds.

The following is an introduction to the meanings of these security threat types: MALWARE, UNWANTED_SOFTWARE, and SOCIAL_ENGINEERING:
- **MALWARE (Malicious Software)**: 
    - **Definition**: Malicious software refers to the general term for software programs that are deliberately programmed or set with malicious purposes, such as aiming to damage the functions and data of computer systems or obtain users' private information. 
    - **Examples**: 
        - **Virus**: It can self-replicate and spread to other programs or files. For example, the once prevalent "Blaster" virus exploited vulnerabilities in the Windows system to spread, which could cause problems such as the system restarting repeatedly and running more slowly. 
        - **Worm**: It can run independently and spread automatically through the network. For instance, the "Nimda" worm virus could spread rapidly in the network, occupying a large amount of network bandwidth and affecting the normal use of the network. 
        - **Trojan Horse**: It disguises itself as a normal program or file to induce users to download and install it. Once it runs, it will perform malicious operations in the background, such as stealing users' account passwords and other information. For example, some Trojan programs disguised as popular games may steal users' account information after the users install them. 
- **UNWANTED_SOFTWARE (Unwanted Software)**: 
    - **Definition**: This type of software is usually not actively expected to be installed by users. They may be installed on devices without the users' knowledge or explicit consent and may bring various troubles and potential risks to users. 
    - **Examples**: 
        - **Adware**: It frequently pops up a large number of advertisement windows, interfering with the normal use of the device by users. These advertisements may occupy system resources, causing the device to run more slowly. Some advertisements may also pose security risks, and clicking on them may lead users to malicious websites. 
        - **Spyware**: It collects users' personal information, browsing habits and other data without the users' awareness and sends this data to third parties. For example, some spyware will record the search keywords entered by users in the browser, the websites visited, etc., infringing on users' privacy. 
        - **Bundled Software**: It is often installed bundled with the software that users actually need. For example, when users download a certain legitimate software, the installation package may be bundled with some other software. These bundled software may be useless in function or even pose security risks. 
- **SOCIAL_ENGINEERING (Social Engineering Attacks)**: 
    - **Definition**: It takes advantage of human psychological weaknesses, trust relationships, and behavioral habits. Through means such as deception and inducement, it obtains sensitive information (such as account passwords, bank card numbers, etc.) or gets users to perform certain operations that are not conducive to their own security. 
    - **Examples**: 
        - **Phishing Email**: The attacker disguises as a legitimate institution (such as a bank, a well-known company, etc.) and sends an email to the user. The email usually contains false links or attachments to induce the user to click. For example, a phishing email disguised as a bank will claim that there is a problem with the user's account and ask the user to click on the link to log in to the "bank website" to modify the information. And this link points to a forged website used to steal the user's account password. 
        - **Telephone Fraud**: The fraudster calls the user, fabricating various reasons (such as winning a prize, being suspected of illegal crimes, etc.) to induce the user to transfer money or disclose personal sensitive information. For example, the scammer calls and claims that the user has won a huge prize, but needs to pay a certain handling fee first to receive the bonus, inducing the user to transfer money. 
        - **Impersonating Customer Service**: The attacker impersonates the customer service staff of a well-known e-commerce platform or other services to contact the user. Under the pretext of solving problems, they obtain the user's account information or defraud money. For example, impersonating a customer service of an e-commerce platform and claiming that there is a problem with the user's order and needs to be refunded, guiding the user to click on a link to operate, but actually defrauding the user's funds.

1. **Principle of Luminance Calculation**:
   - In web design and color theory, an approximate method is usually used to calculate the relative luminance of RGB colors. For an RGB color value `#RRGGBB`, the luminance calculation formula is:
     - \(L = 0.2126\times R + 0.7152\times G+ 0.0722\times B\), where \(R\), \(G\), and \(B\) are the values of the red, green, and blue channels, ranging from \(0\) to \(255\). The larger the calculated \(L\) value, the higher the luminance of the color.
2. **Calculate the Luminance of Three Colors Separately**:
   - **For color `#25098A`**:
     - \(R = 37\), \(G = 9\), \(B = 138\).
     - \(L_1 = 0.2126\times37 + 0.7152\times9 + 0.0722\times138\)
     - \(L_1 = 7.8662 + 6.4368 + 9.9636\)
     - \(L_1 = 24.2666\)
   - **For color `#FF5733`**:
     - \(R = 255\), \(G = 87\), \(B = 51\).
     - \(L_2 = 0.2126\times255 + 0.7152\times87 + 0.0722\times51\)
     - \(L_2 = 54.213 + 62.2224 + 3.6822\)
     - \(L_2 = 120.1176\)
   - **For color `#33FF57`**:
     - \(R = 51\), \(G = 255\), \(B = 87\).
     - \(L_3 = 0.2126\times51 + 0.7152\times255 + 0.0722\times87\)
     - \(L_3 = 10.8426 + 182.376 + 6.2814\)
     - \(L_3 = 199.5\)

3. **Compare Luminance Values**:
   - Compare \(L_1 = 24.2666\), \(L_2 = 120.1176\), \(L_3 = 199.5\).
   - It can be concluded that \(L_3\gt L_2\gt L_1\).

Therefore, the color with the highest luminance among the three is `#33FF57`.

1. **nslookup** 
In the command prompt or terminal of Windows or Linux systems, enter the command `nslookup example.com`. For example:
```bash
nslookup example.com
Server:         192.168.1.1
Address:        192.168.1.1#53

Non-authoritative answer:
Name:   example.com
Address: 93.184.216.34
```
This will return the IP address resolved by the domain name. However, a single query may not display all IPs (if there are multiple).

2. **dig** 
A more powerful DNS query tool in Linux systems. Use the command `dig example.com +short`. For example:
```bash
dig example.com +short
93.184.216.34
```
The `+short` parameter will make the output only display the IP address part of the query result, which is concise and clear.

### Online Tools

2. **WhatIsMyIPAddress**: The [WhatIsMyIPAddress website](https://whatismyipaddress.com/dns-lookup) provides a domain name query function. After entering the domain name, you can see the IP address information it resolves to.

Check other IP addresses of the domain name.

If you only know the domain name “example.com” and want to query the other IP addresses it resolves to, you can use the following common methods:

### Command-line Tools
1. **nslookup** 
In the command prompt or terminal of Windows or Linux systems, enter the command `nslookup example.com`. For example:
```bash
nslookup example.com
Server:         192.168.1.1
Address:        192.168.1.1#53

Non-authoritative answer:
Name:   example.com
Address: 93.184.216.34
```
This will return the IP address resolved by the domain name. However, a single query may not display all IPs (if there are multiple).

2. **dig** 
A more powerful DNS query tool in Linux systems. Use the command `dig example.com +short`. For example:
```bash
dig example.com +short
93.184.216.34
```
The `+short` parameter will make the output only display the IP address part of the query result, which is concise and clear.

### Online Tools
1. **MXToolbox**: Visit the [MXToolbox website](https://mxtoolbox.com/), enter the domain name in the search box. It can provide rich DNS record information, including A records (IP addresses), MX records, etc. You can not only find the currently resolved IP address but also perform other DNS-related diagnostics.
2. **WhatIsMyIPAddress**: The [WhatIsMyIPAddress website](https://whatismyipaddress.com/dns-lookup) provides a domain name query function. After entering the domain name, you can see the IP address information it resolves to.
Query other IP addresses with the same geographical location.

To query other IP addresses in the same geographical location as a certain IP (such as 192.0.2.1, located in Los Angeles, California, USA), you can use the following methods:

### Using Professional Databases and Platforms
 - **MaxMind**:
    - **Introduction**: Provides a GeoIP database with geographical location information accurate to the city level. You can download its free or paid version of the database and then query other IP addresses in the same region as the target IP programmatically (such as using the `geoip2` library in Python).
    - **Steps**:
        1. Download the GeoIP database from the MaxMind official website (https://www.maxmind.com/) (the free GeoLite2 database has certain limitations but can meet basic needs).
        2. Install the `geoip2` library: Run `pip install geoip2` in the command line.
        3. Use the following example code to query IPs in the same region (this is just for illustration and actually needs to be adjusted according to the content and structure of the database):
```python
import geoip2.database

reader = geoip2.database.Reader('path/to/GeoLite2-City.mmdb')
target_ip = '192.0.2.1'
response = reader.city(target_ip)
city_name = response.city.name
country_name = response.country.name

# Assume you have a dataset containing a large number of IPs and their geographical information (simulated here)
ip_geo_data = [
    ('1.2.3.4', 'USA', 'California', 'Los Angeles'),
    ('5.6.7.8', 'USA', 'New York State', 'New York'),
    ('9.10.11.12', 'USA', 'California', 'Los Angeles')
]

for ip, country, state, city in ip_geo_data:
    if country == country_name and state == response.subdivisions.most_specific.name and city == city_name:
        print(ip)

reader.close()
```
 - **IPIP.net**:
    - **Introduction**: Provides online query and offline database services and can also provide detailed IP geographical location information. You can register for an account to obtain an API key and achieve the function of querying IPs in the same region by calling its API.
    - **Steps**:
        1. Register and log in to an IPIP.net account to obtain an API key.
        2. Construct a request according to its API documentation (https://www.ipip.net/ipdb-api.html). For example, use the `requests` library in Python to send a request to obtain IPs in the same region:
```python
import requests

api_key = 'your_api_key'
target_ip = '192.0.2.1'
url = f'https://api.ipip.net/ip?ip={target_ip}&key={api_key}'
response = requests.get(url)
data = response.json()
if data.get('status') =='success':
    target_country = data.get('country')
    target_region = data.get('region')
    target_city = data.get('city')

    # Send another request to obtain IPs in the same region (assuming this query method is supported, actually adjust according to the documentation)
    query_url = f'https://api.ipip.net/ip?country={target_country}&region={target_region}&city={target_city}&key={api_key}'
    query_response = requests.get(query_url)
    query_data = query_response.json()
    if query_data.get('status') =='success':
        for ip_info in query_data.get('data', []):
            print(ip_info.get('ip'))
```

### Network Scanning Tools (with certain limitations and may involve legal issues)
 - **Nmap**:
    - **Introduction**: It is a network scanning tool that can scan hosts within a specified network segment, obtain their IP addresses, and infer their geographical locations through some technologies (but with limited accuracy). If you know the approximate network segment where the target IP is located, you can use Nmap to scan that network segment to find IPs that are more likely to be in the same geographical location.
    - **Steps**: For example, assume that the network segment where the target IP 192.0.2.1 is located may be 192.0.2.0/24. Run `nmap -sn 192.0.2.0/24` in the command line to scan the active hosts within that network segment. Nmap will return a list of discovered IPs. Then combine with other geolocation tools or databases (such as MaxMind mentioned above) to confirm whether these IPs are in the same geographical location as the target IP. However, in an enterprise or public network environment, scanning without authorization may violate regulations or even laws.

inference_output.content:
Below is a quick rundown of the public‑transport options that can get you from downtown Ottawa to the Ottawa International Airport (YOW).  

### 1. Direct service – **Bus 97 (Airport Express)**
* **What it is:** The only OC Transpo route that runs **directly** from downtown (Parliament, Lyon, or Mackenzie‑King stations) to the airport without any transfers.  
* **Frequency:** Every 15 minutes during peak periods, every 30 minutes off‑peak.  
* **Travel time:** About 30 minutes from the downtown stations to the airport terminal.  

> **Bottom line:** If you want a **single‑bus ride** with no transfers, Bus 97 is the only option.

---

### 2. Routes that can get you to the airport **with a transfer** (useful if you miss a 97, need a different departure time, or prefer a different walking distance)

| First bus (downtown) | Where you get off | Transfer to | Approx. total travel time* |
|----------------------|-------------------|-------------|----------------------------|
| **Bus 61** (Parliament → Hurdman) | Hurdman Station | Bus 97 (Hurdman → Airport) | 45 min |
| **Bus 75** (Lyon → Hurdman) | Hurdman Station | Bus 97 (Hurdman → Airport) | 45 min |
| **Bus 98** (Mackenzie‑King → Hurdman) | Hurdman Station | Bus 97 (Hurdman → Airport) | 45 min |

*Times include a short walk (≈5‑7 min) from the downtown O‑Train station to the bus stop, the first‑leg bus ride (≈20‑25 min), the transfer walk at Hurdman (≈2 min), and the final 30‑minute leg on Bus 97.

#### How these work in practice
1. **Walk** a few minutes from your downtown location to the nearest O‑Train (Confederation Line) station (Parliament, Lyon, or Mackenzie‑King).  
2. **Take the O‑Train** one stop east to the station listed above.  
3. **Catch the indicated bus** (61, 75, or 98) to **Hurdman**.  
4. **Transfer** at Hurdman to **Bus 97** for the final leg to the airport.

These alternatives are handy if:
* You’re already on a bus that’s heading toward Hurdman and want to avoid waiting for a 97.
* You missed the last 97 of the day (the O‑Train runs later than the 97 on some evenings).
* You prefer a slightly shorter walk to the downtown station.

---

### 3. Train options
* **OC Transpo’s O‑Train (Confederation Line)** does **not** go to the airport, and there is no commuter‑rail service that reaches YOW.  
* The nearest inter‑city train (Via Rail) stops at **Ottawa Station**, which is still downtown, so you would still need a bus or taxi for the final leg.

---

### 4. Quick “what‑if” checklist

| Situation | Recommended route |
|-----------|-------------------|
| **You want a single ride, no transfers** | **Bus 97** (direct) |
| **You’re already on a bus heading toward Hurdman** | Stay on that bus, then transfer to **Bus 97** at Hurdman |
| **You missed the last 97 of the day** | Take the **O‑Train** to **Hurdman**, then catch the **last 97** (the 97 runs later than most other routes) |
| **You need a wheelchair‑accessible ride** | All OC Transpo buses (including 97, 61, 75, 98) are low‑floor and wheelchair‑accessible. The O‑Train stations are also accessible. |
| **You prefer the shortest walk from downtown** | Use **Bus 61** from **Parliament Station** (≈300 m walk) or **Bus 75** from **Lyon Station** (≈400 m walk). |

---

### TL;DR
* **Only Bus 97** provides a **direct, no‑transfer** connection from downtown Ottawa to the airport.  
* If you’re willing to make **one transfer**, you can reach the airport via **Bus 61, 75, or 98** to Hurdman, then hop on **Bus 97** for the final leg.  
* There are **no train routes** that go to the airport.

Let me know if you’d like a detailed schedule for any of the above routes (e.g., next‑bus times for Bus 61, 75, 98, or the 97), or if you need help planning a specific departure time!

candidate_0_answer_function_list.observation:
## Query the TTL record of a domain name in DNS.

### 1. Query using command-line tools (taking Windows system as an example)
You can use the `nslookup` or `dig` commands.
 - **nslookup**:
    ```
    nslookup
    set type=A
    example.com
    ```
    In the output result, information similar to the following will be displayed:
    ```
    Server:  UnKnown
    Address:  192.168.1.1

    Name:    example.com
    Address:  172.16.254.1
    TTL: 3600
    ```
    Here, `TTL: 3600`, and 3600 seconds is the TTL value of the A record of this domain name.

 - **dig**: If the `dig` tool is not installed on the Windows system, you can obtain it from the [BIND 9](https://www.isc.org/downloads/bind/) installation package. After installation, run the following command in the command line:
    ```
    dig example.com A
    ```
    Find the following part in the output result:
    ```
    example.com.  3600 IN A 172.16.254.1
    ```
    Among them, 3600 is the TTL value.

### 2. Query using online tools
There are many online DNS query tools, such as [MXToolbox](https://mxtoolbox.com/).
 - After opening the website, enter the domain name `example.com` to be queried in the search box.
 - Select the query type as relevant record types such as A record, and the TTL value will be displayed in the query result.

The TTL value represents the time that the record can be cached in the domain name system cache. After this time, the record in the cache will be considered expired and needs to be retrieved from the authoritative DNS server again.

### Basic Information of Salmon

Salmon is a fish widely distributed in the North Pacific and North Atlantic oceans and belongs to the family Salmonidae. They are known for their migrations. Usually, they are born in freshwater, migrate to the ocean to live, and then return to freshwater to spawn.

#### Introduction to Subspecies of Salmon:
1. **Atlantic Salmon (Salmo salar)**: Mainly distributed in the North Atlantic Ocean and commonly found in rivers in Europe and North America.
2. **Sockeye Salmon (Oncorhynchus nerka)**: Mainly distributed in the North Pacific Ocean, especially in the waters of Alaska and Canada.
3. **Coho Salmon (Oncorhynchus kisutch)**: Distributed in the North Pacific Ocean and commonly found on the west coast of the United States and in Japan.

#### Pictures of Salmon:
-![Salmon swimming](https://example.com/salmon1.jpg) A salmon swimming in a river.
-![Close-up of salmon](https://example.com/salmon2.jpg) A close-up shot of a salmon, showing its silver scales.

### Population Status and Sustainability Ratings of Salmon in North America

- **Atlantic Salmon**: The status is endangered, and the sustainability rating is low.
- **Pacific Salmon**: The status is stable, and the sustainability rating is medium.
- **Sockeye Salmon**: The status is stable, and the sustainability rating is high.

The above information shows that in North America, Atlantic Salmon is facing challenges, while Sockeye Salmon has better sustainability.

Values can vary slightly by species (e.g., Atlantic vs. Pacific) and whether the fish is farmed or wild, but the numbers shown are representative of wild‑caught salmon, which is often the benchmark for “clean” nutrition.

| Nutrient | Amount (per 100 g) | % Daily Value* |
|----------|-------------------|----------------|

| **Selenium** | 36 µg | 65 % |
| **Phosphorus** | 200 mg | 20 % |
| **Magnesium** | 29 mg | 7 % |
| **Iron** | 0.8 mg | 4 % |
| **Zinc** | 0.6 mg | 4 % |

\*Percent Daily Values are based on a 2,000‑calorie diet. Your needs may be higher or lower.

### Key Highlights

| Component | Why It Matters |
|-----------|----------------|
| **High‑quality protein** | Provides all essential amino acids; supports muscle maintenance and repair. |
| **Omega‑3 fatty acids (EPA & DHA)** | 2–3 g per 100 g of wild salmon; linked to reduced inflammation, improved heart health, brain function, and eye health. |
| **Vitamin D** | One of the richest natural food sources; essential for bone health, immune function, and mood regulation. |
| **Vitamin B12** | Crucial for red‑blood‑cell formation, nerve health, and DNA synthesis. |
| **Selenium** | A potent antioxidant that helps protect cells from oxidative damage. |
| **Low carbohydrate, low sodium** | Makes salmon a great option for low‑carb, low‑sodium dietary patterns. |

### Farmed vs. Wild Salmon (Quick Comparison)

| Feature | Wild‑caught | Farmed |
|---------|-------------|--------|
| **Calories** | ~142 kcal | ~200 kcal (more fat) |
| **Total Fat** | 6 g | 10–13 g |
| **Omega‑3 (EPA/DHA)** | 2.5 g | 1.5–2 g (still high, but a slightly lower ratio of omega‑3 to omega‑6) |
| **Omega‑6** | ~0.3 g | 2–4 g (higher) |
| **Vitamin D** | 13 µg (520 IU) | 5–10 µg (200–400 IU) |
| **Contaminants** | Generally low; depends on region | May contain higher levels of PCBs or dioxins in some regions; reputable certifications (e.g., ASC, BAP) mitigate this. |

> **Bottom line:** Whether wild or responsibly farmed, salmon remains a nutrient‑dense food, especially prized for its omega‑3 fatty acids, vitamin D, and high‑quality protein.

### Practical Tips for Maximizing Nutrition

1. **Portion size:** A typical serving is 3–4 oz (85–115 g). That provides roughly 150–200 kcal and 20–25 g of protein.
2. **Cooking method:** Grill, bake, poach, or steam to preserve omega‑3s. Avoid deep‑frying, which adds unnecessary saturated fat and can degrade delicate nutrients.
3. **Pairings:** Serve with vitamin‑C‑rich vegetables (e.g., bell peppers, broccoli) to enhance iron absorption, and with a squeeze of lemon for extra flavor and antioxidants.
4. **Storage:** Keep raw salmon refrigerated (≤ 4 °C) and use within 1–2 days, or freeze for longer storage. Thaw in the fridge, not at room temperature, to maintain texture and safety.

### Sources & Further Reading

- USDA FoodData Central, “Salmon, raw, wild, Atlantic” (Nutrient Database).  
- National Institutes of Health (NIH) Office of Dietary Supplements – **Omega‑3 Fatty Acids** fact sheet.  
- American Heart Association – **Fish and Omega‑3 Fatty Acids**.  
- Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) – **Sustainability and Nutrition of Farmed vs. Wild Salmon**.

inference_output.content:
### PM2.5 – Fine Particulate Matter (≤ 2.5 µm)

**What it is**  
PM2.5 refers to airborne particles that are 2.5 micrometers in diameter or smaller—about 30 times smaller than a human hair. Because of their tiny size, these particles can stay suspended in the air for days to weeks and can travel long distances.

**Common Sources**  
| Source Category | Typical Examples |
|-----------------|------------------|
| **Combustion** | Vehicle exhaust (especially diesel), gasoline engines, wood‑burning stoves, wildfires, industrial boilers, power plants |
| **Industrial Processes** | Metal smelting, cement production, oil refining, chemical manufacturing, construction activities (dust that becomes fine) |
| **Secondary Formation** | Gases such as sulfur dioxide (SO₂), nitrogen oxides (NOₓ), and volatile organic compounds (VOCs) react in the atmosphere to form fine particles (e.g., sulfates, nitrates, organic aerosols) |
| **Natural Sources** | Dust from soil erosion, sea spray, volcanic ash, pollen (when broken down to fine fragments) |

**Why PM2.5 Matters for Health**  
- **Deep Lung Penetration**: Particles this small can bypass the nose and throat, reaching the bronchioles and alveoli (the deepest parts of the lungs).  
- **Systemic Effects**: Once deposited, they can cross into the bloodstream, affecting the heart, brain, and other organs.  
- **Acute Impacts**: Short‑term exposure (hours to days) can aggravate asthma, cause coughing, wheezing, shortness of breath, and increase hospital admissions for respiratory and cardiovascular events.  
- **Chronic Impacts**: Long‑term exposure (months to years) is linked to reduced lung function, development of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), heart disease, stroke, and premature mortality. Certain components (e.g., black carbon, heavy metals) are also carcinogenic.  

**Regulatory Standards (U.S.)**  
- **EPA National Ambient Air Quality Standard (NAAQS)** for PM2.5:  
  - **Annual average**: ≤ 12 µg/m³ (primary and secondary standard)  
  - **24‑hour average**: ≤ 35 µg/m³ (primary and secondary standard)  
- **Air Quality Index (AQI) Breakpoints** (U.S. EPA):  
  - 0‑50 = Good (0‑12 µg/m³)  
  - 51‑100 = Moderate (12.1‑35.4 µg/m³)  
  - 101‑150 = Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups (35.5‑55.4 µg/m³)  
  - …and higher categories for increasingly hazardous levels.  

**Typical Mitigation Strategies**  
1. **Transportation** – Promote electric vehicles, improve public transit, enforce stricter emissions standards for diesel engines.  
2. **Industrial Controls** – Install particulate filters (e.g., baghouses, electrostatic precipitators), switch to cleaner fuels, adopt best‑available control technologies (BACT).  
3. **Energy Production** – Shift from coal‑fired power plants to natural gas, renewables, and implement scrubbers/filters on existing plants.  
4. **Residential** – Encourage use of low‑emission wood stoves, improve home heating efficiency, limit open burning.  
5. **Urban Planning** – Increase green spaces and tree canopy, which can capture and settle fine particles.  

**Key Take‑away**  
PM2.5 is a critical air‑quality pollutant because its small size allows it to penetrate deep into the respiratory system and even enter the bloodstream, posing serious short‑ and long‑term health risks. Monitoring its levels (as reflected in today’s AQI of 75, “Moderate”) and implementing emission‑reduction measures are essential steps for protecting public health, especially in densely populated areas like Los Angeles.

PM2.5 refers to particulate matter in the ambient air with an aerodynamic equivalent diameter of 2.5 micrometers or less, and is also known as fine particulate matter. The following is a detailed introduction for you:
### 1. Physical characteristics
 - **Tiny particle size**: 2.5 micrometers is about 1/20 of the diameter of a human hair. Such a small particle size allows them to remain suspended in the air for a long time and is not easily deposited.
 - **Rich in various components**: The composition of PM2.5 is very complex, including organic carbon, elemental carbon, nitrates, sulfates, ammonium salts, etc., and may also adsorb harmful substances such as heavy metals and microorganisms.

### 2. Main sources
 - **Natural sources**: Windblown dust in nature, volcanic ash produced by volcanic eruptions, and smoke and dust generated by forest fires can all form PM2.5. For example, in northern China in spring, sand and dust weather can cause a significant increase in the PM2.5 concentration in the air.
 - **Anthropogenic sources**: This is the main source of PM2.5 and covers multiple fields. During industrial production processes, waste gases emitted by enterprises in industries such as steel, cement, and chemical engineering contain a large amount of fine particulate matter. Motor vehicle exhaust emissions are also an important source. PM2.5 is produced when a car engine burns gasoline or diesel. In addition, the burning of fossil fuels such as coal and oil, including activities such as power generation in power plants and residential heating and cooking, also releases PM2.5.

### 3. Impact on the environment
 - **Reduce atmospheric visibility**: PM2.5 scatters and absorbs sunlight, hindering the propagation of light, resulting in a decrease in atmospheric visibility, affecting traffic safety, and prone to causing haze weather. In some big cities, haze weather occurs frequently, seriously affecting people's travel and the normal operation of the city.
 - **Affect climate change**: PM2.5 can change the earth's radiation balance. On the one hand, some particulate matter can reflect solar radiation, reducing the amount of solar heat reaching the ground. On the other hand, some particulate matter can absorb heat, affecting the temperature distribution and circulation of the atmosphere, and thus having a complex impact on the global climate.

### 4. Hazards to human health
 - **Trigger respiratory diseases**: Due to the small particle size of PM2.5, it can directly enter the deep part of the human respiratory tract, even reach the alveoli, and deposit in the alveoli. Long-term exposure can damage the respiratory mucosa, causing symptoms such as coughing, wheezing, and difficulty breathing, and increasing the risk of respiratory diseases such as asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
 - **Affect the cardiovascular system**: Harmful substances in PM2.5 can enter the human cardiovascular system through the blood circulation, leading to vascular endothelial dysfunction, increased blood viscosity, elevated blood pressure, etc., and thus increasing the incidence of cardiovascular diseases such as coronary heart disease, myocardial infarction, and arrhythmia.

* **GDP** grew sharply from a contraction in 2020 (‑3.4 % growth) to a strong rebound in 2021 (+5.7 %). Growth slowed to modest levels in 2022 (+2.1 %) and 2023 (+2.5 %).

The following is detailed information about USDT:

### Basic Definition
USDT is a stablecoin. It aims to maintain a relatively stable value by pegging to a certain asset (usually fiat currency, such as the US dollar). Its original design intention was to solve the problem of large price fluctuations in the cryptocurrency market, allowing users to have a relatively stable value reference and trading medium when trading cryptocurrencies.

### Issuance and Operation Mechanism
 - **Issuer**: USDT is issued by Tether. Tether claims that each USDT is backed by corresponding fiat currency (mainly US dollars) reserves, that is, it implements a 1:1 reserve system. This means that for every 1 USDT issued, there is 1 US dollar in its reserve account.
 - **Verification Method**: Although Tether claims to have sufficient fiat currency reserves, the transparency of its reserve situation has been questioned in the past. However, in recent years, it has also been audited to some extent to try to enhance market trust. Its operation relies on blockchain technology and currently supports multiple blockchain networks, such as Omni (based on the Bitcoin blockchain), ERC - 20 (based on the Ethereum blockchain), TRC - 20 (based on the Tron blockchain), etc. USDT on different networks essentially represents the same value, but there may be differences in transfer speed, handling fees, etc.

### Market Applications
 - **Trading Medium**: In the cryptocurrency trading market, USDT is widely used as the quoting currency for trading pairs. Due to the large price fluctuations among cryptocurrencies, using USDT as an intermediate medium can facilitate the trading and price measurement of different cryptocurrencies. For example, when you want to exchange BTC for ETH, you can first exchange BTC for USDT and then use USDT to buy ETH.
 - **Hedging Tool**: When the cryptocurrency market experiences a significant decline, investors often exchange their cryptocurrencies for USDT to temporarily avoid price fluctuation risks and wait for the market situation to improve before re - entering the market.

### Advantages
 - **Relatively Stable Price**: Compared with the large price fluctuations of other cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin and Ethereum, the price of USDT is relatively stable. This gives it certain advantages in trading and asset storage, especially for investors who want to conduct short - term trading in the cryptocurrency market or need to hold assets of stable value temporarily.
 - **High Liquidity**: Due to its wide application and market acceptance, USDT has high liquidity on major cryptocurrency exchanges and can be quickly bought and sold.

### Risks

The following is detailed information about USDT:

### Basic Definition
USDT is a stablecoin. It aims to maintain a relatively stable value by pegging to a certain asset (usually fiat currency, such as the US dollar). Its original design intention was to solve the problem of large price fluctuations in the cryptocurrency market, allowing users to have a relatively stable value reference and trading medium when trading cryptocurrencies.

### Issuance and Operation Mechanism
 - **Issuer**: USDT is issued by Tether. Tether claims that each USDT is backed by corresponding fiat currency (mainly US dollars) reserves, that is, it implements a 1:1 reserve system. This means that for every 1 USDT issued, there is 1 US dollar in its reserve account.
 - **Verification Method**: Although Tether claims to have sufficient fiat currency reserves, the transparency of its reserve situation has been questioned in the past. However, in recent years, it has also been audited to some extent to try to enhance market trust. Its operation relies on blockchain technology and currently supports multiple blockchain networks, such as Omni (based on the Bitcoin blockchain), ERC - 20 (based on the Ethereum blockchain), TRC - 20 (based on the Tron blockchain), etc. USDT on different networks essentially represents the same value, but there may be differences in transfer speed, handling fees, etc.

### Market Applications
 - **Trading Medium**: In the cryptocurrency trading market, USDT is widely used as the quoting currency for trading pairs. Due to the large price fluctuations among cryptocurrencies, using USDT as an intermediate medium can facilitate the trading and price measurement of different cryptocurrencies. For example, when you want to exchange BTC for ETH, you can first exchange BTC for USDT and then use USDT to buy ETH.
 - **Hedging Tool**: When the cryptocurrency market experiences a significant decline, investors often exchange their cryptocurrencies for USDT to temporarily avoid price fluctuation risks and wait for the market situation to improve before re - entering the market.

### Advantages
 - **Relatively Stable Price**: Compared with the large price fluctuations of other cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin and Ethereum, the price of USDT is relatively stable. This gives it certain advantages in trading and asset storage, especially for investors who want to conduct short - term trading in the cryptocurrency market or need to hold assets of stable value temporarily.
 - **High Liquidity**: Due to its wide application and market acceptance, USDT has high liquidity on major cryptocurrency exchanges and can be quickly bought and sold.

### Risks
 - **Trust Risk**: Although Tether promises that USDT has sufficient fiat currency reserves, if there are problems with its reserve situation, such as insufficient reserves, it may lead to the inability of USDT to maintain a 1:1 peg with the US dollar, thereby triggering market panic and investor losses.
 - **Regulatory Risk**: With the strengthening of global regulation of cryptocurrencies, stablecoins are also facing increasingly strict regulatory reviews. If there are unfavorable changes in regulatory policies, it may affect the issuance, trading, and use of USDT, and thus affect its market value and liquidity.

Below is a curated “who’s‑who” of the most influential and up‑and‑coming researchers, engineers, and thought‑leaders whose work shapes the deep‑learning‑for‑NLP landscape surveyed in **“Deep Learning for Natural Language Processing: A Survey”** (arXiv:2104.12345).  I have grouped them by the major technology themes that dominate the field today, and added a short note on each person’s signature contributions, current affiliation, and why they are considered a cutting‑edge talent.

---

## 1. Foundations of Deep Learning & Transformers  

| Name | Affiliation (2024) | Signature Contributions | Why a Cutting‑Edge Talent |
|------|-------------------|--------------------------|---------------------------|
| **Yoshua Bengio** | Université de Montréal (Mila) | Pioneered deep representation learning; co‑author of the original *Neural Machine Translation* (NMT) paper; mentor of many transformer researchers. | Nobel‑level influence on the theoretical underpinnings of modern NLP models. |
| **Geoffrey Hinton** | University of Toronto / Google Brain | Back‑propagation, deep belief networks, and the *“capsule”* ideas that inspired attention mechanisms. | Continues to guide research on efficient, sparse deep models. |
| **Yann LeCun** | NYU / Meta AI | Convolutional nets → “self‑supervised” learning; early work on sequence modeling that fed into transformer design. | Drives the push toward self‑supervised pre‑training for language. |
| **Ashish Vaswani** | Google DeepMind | Co‑author of the *Attention Is All You Need* (Transformer) paper (2017). | Directly responsible for the architecture that underlies BERT, GPT, T5, etc. |
| **Jacob Devlin** | Google AI | Lead author of **BERT** (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers). | BERT sparked the pre‑training/fine‑tuning paradigm that dominates NLP today. |
| **Alec Radford** | OpenAI | Lead author of **GPT‑1/2/3** series; champion of scaling language models. | Demonstrated the power of massive, unsupervised language models. |
| **Noam Shazeer** | Google Brain | Co‑author of the *Transformer* paper; invented **Sparse Transformer** and **Mixture‑of‑Experts** (MoE) scaling. | Pushing the frontier of model efficiency at scale. |

---

## 2. Large Language Models (LLMs) & Scaling Laws  

| Name | Affiliation | Key Works | Cutting‑Edge Impact |
|------|-------------|-----------|---------------------|
| **Sam Altman** (CEO) | OpenAI | Oversaw development of **GPT‑4** and the ChatGPT product line. | Guides the commercial and research direction of LLMs. |
| **Dario Amodei** | Anthropic | Co‑founder; leads work on **Claude** series and safety‑oriented LLM research. | Pioneering responsible scaling and alignment. |
| **Jianfeng Gao** | Microsoft Research Asia | Co‑author of **Turing‑NLG**, **Turing‑Bletchley**, and **DeepSpeed**. | Advances efficient training/inference for massive models. |
| **Ming‑Wei Chang** | Google DeepMind | Lead on **GLaM** (Generalist Language Model) – a sparsely‑activated MoE LLM. | Demonstrates how to achieve high performance with lower compute. |
| **Sebastian Ruder** | DeepMind (formerly) | Author of the “*Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models*” blog series; curates LLM research. | Provides the community with clear, data‑driven guidance on model scaling. |

---

## 3. Multilingual & Cross‑Lingual NLP  

| Name | Affiliation | Notable Projects | Why They Matter |
|------|-------------|------------------|-----------------|
| **Mona Diab** | Carnegie Mellon University | **MASS**, **XLM‑R**, and multilingual evaluation benchmarks. | Drives research on language‑agnostic representations. |
| **Yoshua Bengio** (again) | Mila | Co‑author of **M2M‑100** (Facebook) and **M2M‑100** multilingual translation. | Bridges the gap between high‑resource and low‑resource languages. |
| **Michele Banko** | Facebook AI Research (FAIR) | **M2M‑100**, **M2M‑100‑large**, and multilingual pre‑training pipelines. | Enables truly universal translation without English pivot. |
| **Graham Neubig** | Carnegie Mellon University | **M2M‑100**, **Zero‑Shot Cross‑Lingual Transfer**, and **Massively Multilingual BERT**. | Focuses on low‑resource language technology. |

---

## 4. Efficient & Green NLP (Model Compression, Distillation, Retrieval‑Augmented Generation)  

| Name | Affiliation | Core Contributions | Cutting‑Edge Relevance |
|------|-------------|--------------------|------------------------|
| **Hugo Larochelle** | Google DeepMind | Co‑author of **DistilBERT**, **TinyBERT**, and knowledge‑distillation frameworks. | Makes powerful models deployable on edge devices. |
| **Yoon Kim** | Harvard University | Developed **ALBERT** (parameter‑efficient BERT) and **ELECTRA** (sample‑efficient pre‑training). | Shows how to retain performance while cutting parameters. |
| **Kyunghyun Cho** | NYU | Co‑inventor of **RNN‑search** and **attention‑based encoder‑decoder**; recent work on **Retrieval‑Augmented Generation (RAG)**. | Bridges classic seq2seq with modern retrieval‑based methods. |
| **Sebastian Ruder** (again) | DeepMind | Author of **AdapterFusion**, **LoRA** (Low‑Rank Adaptation) for fine‑tuning. | Enables parameter‑efficient adaptation of LLMs. |

---

## 5. Responsible AI, Ethics, & Alignment  

| Name | Affiliation | Main Works | Why They’re Critical |
|------|-------------|------------|----------------------|
| **Timnit Gebru** | Distributed AI Research Institute (DAIR) | Papers on bias in language models, **“Datasheets for Datasets”**. | Sets standards for fairness and transparency. |
| **Margaret Mitchell** | Google AI (formerly) | Co‑author of **“Model Cards for Model Reporting”**; research on bias mitigation. | Provides practical tools for responsible deployment. |
| **Dawn Song** | UC Berkeley | Work on **adversarial robustness** for NLP and **secure model training**. | Protects models from malicious exploitation. |
| **Chris Olah** | Anthropic | Research on interpretability (e.g., **“Feature Visualization”** for language models). | Helps us understand what LLMs actually learn. |

---

## 6. Emerging “Rising Stars” (Post‑doc/early‑career researchers making waves in 2023‑2024)

| Name | Institution | Recent Breakthroughs | Why Watch Them |
|------|-------------|----------------------|----------------|
| **Anna Rogers** | University of Copenhagen | **“A Primer in BERTology”** (survey) and work on probing methods for LLMs. | Leading the next generation of model interpretability. |
| **Jing Li** | Stanford University | **“In-Context Learning for Few‑Shot Prompting”**; novel prompting strategies for LLMs. | Pushing the limits of zero‑shot capabilities. |
| **Xiaoya Li** | Carnegie Mellon University | **“Sparse Mixture‑of‑Experts for Efficient LLMs”**; open‑source MoE toolkit. | Making massive models more accessible. |
| **Michele Donini** | University of Pisa | **“Cross‑lingual Retrieval‑Augmented Generation”**; multilingual RAG systems. | Bridging retrieval and generation across languages. |
| **Yashas Annadani** | Google Research | **“Chain‑of‑Thought Prompting”** extensions for reasoning in LLMs. | Enhances logical reasoning in language models. |

---

## 7. How These Talents Shape the Technologies Discussed in the Survey  

| Survey Section | Representative Talent(s) | Typical Contributions to That Section |
|----------------|--------------------------|----------------------------------------|
| **Neural Machine Translation (NMT)** | Ashish Vaswani, Yoon Kim, Mona Diab | Transformer architecture, efficient multilingual NMT models. |
| **Pre‑training & Fine‑tuning Paradigm** | Jacob Devlin, Alec Radford, Yoon Kim, Sebastian Ruder | BERT, GPT, ALBERT, LoRA – the core workflow of modern NLP. |
| **Large‑Scale Language Modeling** | Sam Altman, Dario Amodei, Ming‑Wei Chang, Noam Shazeer | GPT‑4, Claude, GLaM – scaling laws, MoE, safety. |
| **Multilingual & Low‑Resource NLP** | Graham Neubig, Mona Diab, Yashas Annadani | Cross‑lingual transfer, zero‑shot translation, multilingual RAG. |
| **Model Compression & Efficient Inference** | Hugo Larochelle, Yoon Kim, Sebastian Ruder | DistilBERT, ALBERT, LoRA, AdapterFusion – making models lightweight. |
| **Ethics, Fairness, & Alignment** | Timnit Gebru, Margaret Mitchell, Dawn Song, Chris Olah | Bias audits, model cards, interpretability, robustness. |
| **Prompt Engineering & In‑Context Learning** | Jing Li, Yashas Annadani | Chain‑of‑thought prompting, few‑shot learning techniques. |

---

### Quick Takeaway  

- **Visionaries (Bengio, Hinton, LeCun)** set the deep‑learning foundations that made modern NLP possible.

inference_output.content:
Below is a short “highlight‑sheet” that pairs three of the most influential deep‑learning pioneers with one of their landmark papers (one paper per person).  For each work I give the full citation, a brief description of the key contribution, and why it remains a cornerstone of modern deep‑learning research.

| Talent | Representative Paper (one per person) | Year | Venue | Why It’s Cutting‑Edge / Impact |
|--------|----------------------------------------|------|-------|--------------------------------|
| **Geoffrey Hinton** | **“Learning Multiple Layers of Representation”** (with Simon J. Osindero & Yee‑Whye Teh) | 2006 | *Neural Computation* 18(7): 1527‑1540 | Introduced **Deep Belief Networks (DBNs)** and demonstrated that unsupervised layer‑wise pre‑training could effectively initialize deep neural nets, overcoming the “vanishing‑gradient” problem that had stalled deep learning for years. This paper sparked the modern deep‑learning renaissance and paved the way for later breakthroughs in image, speech, and language modeling. |
| **Yann LeCun** | **“Gradient‑Based Learning Applied to Document Recognition”** (with Léon Bottou, Yoshua Bengio & Patrick Haffner) | 1998 | *Proceedings of the IEEE* 86(11): 2278‑2324 | The classic **LeNet‑5** paper that first showed how **convolutional neural networks (CNNs)** could be trained end‑to‑end on large handwritten‑digit datasets (MNIST). It introduced key architectural ideas—local receptive fields, weight sharing, and subsampling—that are still the backbone of today’s vision models (ResNet, EfficientNet, Vision Transformers with hybrid CNN heads, etc.). |
| **Yoshua Bengio** | **“Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate”** (with Dzmitry Bahdanau & Kyunghyun Cho) | 2015 | *International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR)* | While the paper is often credited to the “attention” community, Bengio’s group introduced the **Bahdanau attention mechanism** that lets an encoder‑decoder RNN focus on relevant source words during translation. This breakthrough made **seq2seq** models far more effective and directly inspired the Transformer architecture (Vaswani et al., 2017), which now dominates NLP, speech, and even vision. |
| **Ian Goodfellow** (added for completeness) | **“Generative Adversarial Nets”** (with Jean Pouget‑Abadie, Mehdi Mirza, Bing Xu, David Warde‑Farley, Sherjil Ozair, Aaron Courville & Yoshua Bengio) | 2014 | *Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)* | Introduced **Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)**, a novel framework where a generator and a discriminator compete in a minimax game. GANs opened an entirely new research direction for high‑fidelity image synthesis, style transfer, data augmentation, and unsupervised representation learning. |
| **Andrew Ng** | **“Sparse Autoencoder”** (with Honglak Lee, Y. Bengio, A. Courville) – *“Unsupervised Feature Learning and Deep Learning Tutorial”* (2006) | 2006 | *Technical Report, Stanford* | One of the earliest practical demonstrations that **deep unsupervised feature learning** (via stacked autoencoders) could dramatically improve performance on vision tasks. Ng’s work helped popularize deep learning in the broader machine‑learning community and inspired many later “pre‑training” approaches. |

### How to Use These Papers

| Use‑Case | Suggested Approach |
|----------|--------------------|
| **Getting started with deep nets** | Read LeCun’s 1998 LeNet paper to understand convolutional layers, then implement a simple CNN on MNIST. |
| **Understanding unsupervised pre‑training** | Study Hinton’s DBN paper; try layer‑wise Restricted Boltzmann Machine (RBM) pre‑training on a small dataset before fine‑tuning. |
| **Sequence modeling & attention** | Follow the 2015 Bahdanau et al. paper; implement an encoder‑decoder with attention in PyTorch/TensorFlow, then experiment with the Transformer. |
| **Generative modeling** | Dive into the 2014 GAN paper; start with the original DCGAN architecture and explore conditional GANs for image‑to‑image translation. |
| **Practical tutorials** | Andrew Ng’s sparse autoencoder notes are a concise, code‑first guide for building deep unsupervised models. |

These five papers collectively illustrate the evolution of deep learning from **convolutional vision models**, through **unsupervised representation learning**, to **sequence‑to‑sequence attention**, and finally to **adversarial generative modeling**—the core technologies that underpin today’s state‑of‑the‑art AI systems.

inference_output.content:
**Step 1 – Resolve the domain name**

I used the `resolveIPHostname` tool to look up the A‑record for **example.com**.

```json
{
  "ip_address": "example.com",
  "include_ptr": "no"
}
```

**Result**

```
example.com → 93.184.216.34
```

---

**Step 2 – Determine the /16 network (subnet mask 255.255.0.0)**  

A mask of `255.255.0.0` is a **/16** network.  
Applying it to the resolved address (93.184.216.34) gives:

| Item                | Value (dotted‑decimal) | Value (binary)                     |
|---------------------|------------------------|------------------------------------|
| **Network address** | 93.184.0.0             | 01011101 10111000 00000000 00000000 |
| **Broadcast address**| 93.184.255.255        | 01011101 10111000 11111111 11111111 |
| **First usable host**| 93.184.0.1            | 01011101 10111000 00000000 00000001 |
| **Last usable host** | 93.184.255.254        | 01011101 10111000 11111111 11111110 |

The **usable host range** therefore spans from **93.184.0.1** to **93.184.255.254**.

---

**Step 3 – How many hosts?**

A /16 network contains:

* **Total IPs:** 2¹⁶ = **65 536**
* **Usable hosts:** 65 536 − 2 (network + broadcast) = **65 534**

Listing every single host address (and its binary form) would produce 65 534 lines, which is far too large for a normal response.  

---

**Step 4 – Sample conversion to binary**

Below are the first five and the last five usable host addresses, shown in both dotted‑decimal and binary notation.

| # | Dotted‑decimal | Binary (8‑bit octets) |
|---|----------------|-----------------------|
| 1 | 93.184.0.1     | 01011101 10111000 00000000 00000001 |
| 2 | 93.184.0.2     | 01011101 10111000 00000000 00000010 |
| 3 | 93.184.0.3     | 01011101 10111000 00000000 00000011 |
| 4 | 93.184.0.4     | 01011101 10111000 00000000 00000100 |
| 5 | 93.184.0.5     | 01011101 10111000 00000000 00000101 |
| … | …              | … |
| 65 530 | 93.184.255.250 | 01011101 10111000 11111111 11111010 |
| 65 531 | 93.184.255.251 | 01011101 10111000 11111111 11111011 |
| 65 532 | 93.184.255.252 | 01011101 10111000 11111111 11111100 |
| 65 533 | 93.184.255.253 | 01011101 10111000 11111111 11111101 |
| 65 534 | 93.184.255.254 | 01011101 10111000 11111111 11111110 |

---

### What you can do with the full list

If you really need **all** 65 534 host addresses in binary, you can generate them programmatically.  
For example, in Python:

```python
import ipaddress

net = ipaddress.ip_network('93.184.0.0/16')
for ip in net.hosts():               # skips network & broadcast
    print(f"{ip}  {bin(int(ip))[2:].zfill(32)}")
```

This script will print every usable IP together with its 32‑bit binary representation.

---

**Summary**

* **Domain:** `example.com` → **IP:** `93.184.216.34`
* **Subnet mask:** `255.255.0.0` → **/16 network** `93.184.0.0/16`
* **Usable host range:** `93.184.0.1` – `93.184.255.254` (65 534 hosts)
* **Binary conversion:** shown for the first/last few hosts; a script can generate the full list if required.

When the subnet mask is 255.255.255.255, it means there is only one address in this network, which is the address itself, and there are no available host addresses.

For the previously queried IP address 93.184.216.34 of `example.com`, in the case of a subnet mask of 255.255.255.255, this network has only this one address, and there are no other additional host addresses available for calculation.

From the perspective of network partitioning, 255.255.255.255 means there are no host bits, and all 32 bits are used to identify the network address. So this IP address 93.184.216.34 is both the network address and the broadcast address, and there is no address space that can be allocated to hosts.

**Nyungwe Forest National Park – A Comprehensive Overview** --- ## 1. Quick Facts | Item | Details | |------|---------| | **Official Name** | Nyungwe Forest National Park | | **Location** | South‑west Rwanda, bordering the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and Burundi. The park’s main entrance is at **Nyamagabe** (formerly Gikongoro). | | **Coordinates** | 2.4808° S, 29.2000° E | | **Size** | ~ 1,015 km² (≈ 247,000 acres) of montane rainforest, bamboo, grassland and swamp. | | **Establishment** | Declared a national park in **2004** (previously a forest reserve since 1933). | | **Governing Body** | Rwanda Development Board (RDB) – Parks and Tourism Division, in partnership with the Rwanda Forestry Authority and local communities. | | **Contact** | Email: **info@nyungwepark.rw** • Phone: **+250 788 123 789** | | **Nearest Towns** | Nyamagabe, Huye (Butare), and the border town of **Cyangugu** (DRC). | | **Altitude Range** | 1,600 m – 2,950 m above sea level (the highest point is **Mount Bigugu**). | | **Climate** | Humid montane; average annual rainfall 1,500–2,500 mm, temperature 12–20 °C. | --- ## 2. Historical Background ### Pre‑colonial Era (Millions of years – 19th century) * **Ancient Rainforest** – Nyungwe is part of the **Albertine Rift** forest block, one of the oldest continuous rainforests in Africa. Pollen and fossil records show that the forest has existed for **over 2 million years**, providing a refuge for countless plant and animal lineages during climatic fluctuations. * **Cultural Landscape** – The forest was a sacred hunting ground for the **Rwanda, Burundi, and Bantu kingdoms** (e.g., the Kingdom of Rwanda under the Nyiginya dynasty). Oral traditions speak of “the forest of spirits,” where chiefs performed rites before hunting expeditions. ### Colonial Period (1890s – 1962) * **German & Belgian Administration** – The area was first surveyed by German colonial officers (late 19th c.) and later administered by the Belgians after World I. In **1933**, the colonial government designated the forest as a **“Forest Reserve”** (Réserve Forestière) to protect timber resources, especially **Coffea arabica** (wild coffee) and **Prunus africana** (African cherry). * **Early Scientific Exploration** – European botanists (e.g., **John H. G. B.** and **E. A. B.** in the 1930s) documented the park’s extraordinary plant diversity, noting over **800 tree species** already. ### Post‑Independence & Conservation Awakening (1962 – 1994) * **Rwanda’s Independence (1962)** – The forest remained a reserve, but logging pressures increased as the country’s population grew. * **1970s–80s** – International NGOs (e.g., **WWF**, **Conservation International**) began field surveys, discovering **high primate endemism** (e.g., the **Ruwenzori colobus**). Their reports sparked the first calls for stricter protection. ### Civil Conflict & Recovery (1994 – 2000) * **Genocide Aftermath** – The 1994 genocide caused massive displacement; many refugees used the forest as a temporary shelter, leading to **illegal hunting and timber extraction**. * **Re‑forestation & Community Programs** – In the late 1990s, the Rwandan government, with UNDP and NGOs, launched **re‑forestation projects** and **community‑based natural resource management** to restore degraded zones. ### National Park Designation (2004 – Present) * **2004** – Nyungwe was officially upgraded from a forest reserve to **Nyungwe Forest National Park**, giving it the highest level of legal protection under Rwandan law. * **2005–2010** – Development of **tourist infrastructure** (canopy walkways, hiking trails, visitor centre) and **research stations** (e.g., the **Nyungwe Research Centre**). * **2010s** – The park became a flagship for **high‑altitude rainforest conservation** in the Albertine Rift, hosting **regional monitoring programs** for climate change, primate health, and forest carbon sequestration. * **2020s** – Ongoing **“Nyungwe 2030”** strategy aims to increase eco‑tourism revenue, expand community‑benefit schemes, and achieve **Zero Poaching** by 2030. --- ## 3. Physical & Ecological Characteristics ### 3.1. Habitat Types | Habitat | Elevation | Key Species | |---------|-----------|-------------| | **Montane Rainforest** | 1,600–2,500 m | *Prunus africana*, *Ruwenzori colobus*, *Rhinolophus* bats, 1,000+ plant species | | **Bamboo Stands** | 1,800–2,300 m | *Bambusa vulgaris*, *Bamboo lemur* (*Hapalemur simus*) | | **High‑Altitude Grasslands & Heath** | 2,300–2,950 m | *Rwanda’s endemic giant lobelia* (*Lobelia rhynchopetalum*), *Rwanda’s antelope* (*Kobus vardonii*) | | **Swamp & Riparian Zones** | Valley bottoms | *Papyrus* (*Cyperus papyrus*), *African dwarf crocodile* (*Osteolaemus tetraspis*) | ### 3.2. **Exchange‑Rate Summary (USD → EUR)**  
| Date (YYYY‑MM‑DD) | Rate (EUR per 1 USD) |
|-------------------|----------------------|
| 2023‑01‑01 | **0.945** |
| 2023‑02‑01 | **0.925** |
| 2023‑03‑01 | **0.935** |
| 2023‑03‑31 | **0.915** |

### 1. Rate movement (Jan 1 – Mar 31 2023)

| Period | Rate change | % change |
|--------|-------------|----------|
| Jan 1 → Mar 31 | 0.915 – 0.945 = **‑0.030** EUR | **‑3.17 %** |
| Jan 1 → Feb 1 | 0.925 – 0.945 = **‑0.020** EUR | **‑2.12 %** |
| Feb 1 → Mar 1 | 0.935 – 0.925 = **+0.010** EUR | **+1.08 %** |
| Mar 1 → Mar 31 | 0.915 – 0.935 = **‑0.020** EUR | **‑2.14 %** |

*Overall, the USD weakened against the euro by about 3 % over the first quarter of 2023.*

### 2. Conversion example – USD 10,000 to EUR

Using the **most recent rate** in the period (2023‑03‑31 = 0.915 EUR/USD):

\[
10{,}000\ \text{USD} \times 0.915\ \frac{\text{EUR}}{\text{USD}} = \mathbf{9{,}150\ EUR}
\]

If the client wanted a quick estimate based on the **average rate** across the four data points:

\[
\text{Average rate} = \frac{0.945 + 0.925 + 0.935 + 0.915}{4} = 0.93\ \text{EUR/USD}
\]

\[
10{,}000\ \text{USD} \times 0.93 = \mathbf{9{,}300\ EUR}
\]

### 3. Take‑aways for the client

* The USD lost roughly **3 %** of its purchasing power against the euro from the start of 2023 to the end of March.
* Converting **USD 10,000** at the end‑of‑quarter rate would yield **≈ €9,150**.
* If the client prefers a more “mid‑point” estimate, using the average rate gives **≈ €9,300**.

Feel free to let me know if you need a more granular daily series, a chart, or a projection based on forward‑rate data.

**Step 1 – Identify the currency with the lowest EUR‑exchange rate**

| Currency | EUR per unit (Jan 18 2025) |
|----------|---------------------------|
| USD      | 0.92 EUR |
| JPY      | **0.0071 EUR** |
| GBP      | 1.15 EUR |

The **Japanese yen (JPY)** has the lowest rate (0.0071 EUR per JPY).

---

**Step 2 – Convert 5 000 JPY to euros**

\[
5 000\ \text{JPY} \times 0.0071\ \frac{\text{EUR}}{\text{JPY}} = 35.5\ \text{EUR}
\]

---

**Step 3 – Convert those euros to US dollars (the “former” currency in the original USD/EUR pair)**  

From the same date (Jan 18 2025) the USD‑to‑EUR rate is 0.92 EUR per USD, i.e.:

\[
1\ \text{USD} = 0.92\ \text{EUR}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
1\ \text{EUR} = \frac{1}{0.92}\ \text{USD} \approx 1.08696\ \text{USD}
\]

\[
35.5\ \text{EUR} \times 1.08696\ \frac{\text{USD}}{\text{EUR}} \approx 38.59\ \text{USD}
\]

---

### Result
- **5 000 JPY** → **35.5 EUR** → **≈ 38.6 USD**

So, using the lowest‑rate currency (JPY) and the original USD/EUR exchange pair, 5 000 yen would purchase **about 38.6 US dollars**.
